openingProblem.problem: In 1994 every South African gained the vote. Four years later the deputy president said the country was still 'two nations', one white and prosperous, the other black and poor. How far did the new democracy's policies change the lives of most South Africans by 2000?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: did policy close the gap between the 'two nations'?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Building a nation: symbols and the TRC
chunks.body:
In 1994 South Africa had been, in Bottaro and Stanley's words, the most divided society in the world. Archbishop Desmond Tutu called the new democracy "the rainbow nation", but turning a people divided by race into one nation was a huge task. The government began with **symbols**. The new national anthem combined the old anthem with the African liberation hymn "Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika", sung in Xhosa, Zulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans and English. A new flag, new public holidays and new monuments commemorated the struggle against apartheid, while old monuments such as the Voortrekker Monument were left standing.

The boldest step was the **Truth and Reconciliation Commission** (TRC), set up in 1996 and chaired by Tutu. Unlike the Nuremberg trials, it was based on **restorative** rather than retributive justice: its purpose was to uncover the truth and so bring about reconciliation. Between 1996 and 1998 more than 22,000 victims told their stories at hearings broadcast live on radio and television. Perpetrators on all sides, including the liberation movements, could receive amnesty if their acts were politically motivated and they made a full disclosure; 1,167 of 7,116 applications were granted. Justice Richard Goldstone argued that trials or a blanket amnesty would each have wrecked the negotiations, and called the TRC "a bridge from the old to the new".

The TRC was controversial. P.W. Botha refused to appear; De Klerk apologised for apartheid but denied authorising the security forces' brutality. The ANC was angry that the TRC treated the crimes of the state and of the liberation movements alike, and applied for amnesty only when Tutu threatened to resign. The final report blamed Botha's government for torture, arson, abduction and sabotage, but also criticised abuses in ANC camps. Some whites denounced the TRC as a witch-hunt, while many black South Africans felt that justice had not been done and victims received little compensation.

This mattered because the TRC exposed the truth without punishing most perpetrators, which meant that it helped secure peace but left many people feeling that reconciliation had come at the expense of justice.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Old monuments remained to reassure whites.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The TRC uncovered the truth through restorative justice.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was not a court and could not punish.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The TRC was criticised from all sides.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Goldstone argued there was no alternative.

chunks.title: From the RDP to GEAR: economic policy
chunks.body:
The ANC's historic programme, the Freedom Charter of 1955, had called for state ownership of key sectors of the economy. By 1994 the ANC had abandoned nationalisation, despite calls for it from its allies the SACP and COSATU. Instead, the Government of National Unity implemented the **Reconstruction and Development Programme** (RDP), an ambitious plan to redistribute wealth: it promised 300,000 new houses a year and access to clean water, sanitation and electricity for the whole population. It soon became clear that its goals were unrealistic, because there was not enough money.

In 1996 the RDP office was closed, and the finance minister **Trevor Manuel** announced the **Growth, Employment and Reconstruction** programme (GEAR). Based on free-market principles, it included the privatisation of state-owned enterprises, and the government hoped it would attract foreign investment, increase exports and create jobs. Business leaders credited Manuel and the Reserve Bank governor Tito Mboweni with creating a stable economy: from 1995 growth averaged 3.2 per cent a year and inflation fell to around 6 per cent.

But neither the RDP nor GEAR created enough jobs. COSATU blamed GEAR's privatisation for the loss, it claimed in 2000, of half a million jobs since 1994. The 2001 census put unemployment at 41.6 per cent. The government did transform **labour relations**: NEDLAC brought government, unions and business together; the Labour Relations Act of 1995 created a body (the CCMA) that handled more than 81,000 disputes in 1998; and strikes declined. The Basic Conditions of Employment Act of 1997 regulated hours and wages, and the Employment Equity Act of 1998 favoured historically disadvantaged workers. Critics saw costs: Nigel Worden notes that wage levels stayed well above those in Asia and Latin America, making South Africa less competitive, and Leonard Thompson that the laws gave unions unusual power.

This mattered because the government chose growth and stability over redistribution, which meant that the economy recovered while unemployment and poverty remained.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: COSATU blamed it for job losses.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Neither the RDP nor GEAR reduced unemployment.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The informal sector employed many people.

chunks.title: Welfare, education and health
chunks.body:
The constitution promised everyone the right to social security, but the government could not afford the level of benefits previously given to whites. Before 1994, 2.6 million people received a grant on racially unequal terms. The new government increased pensions and introduced a **child support grant**. By 2002 seven million people out of forty-five million depended on social grants. Under the RDP, a 2001 government report recorded 1.2 million houses built, more than seven million people given access to free basic water, and 3.5 million electricity connections, though millions still lacked these services.

**Education** was one of apartheid's worst legacies, with fifteen separate education departments and overcrowded, under-resourced black schools. The new government built thousands of schools, made primary schooling compulsory and increased the education budget substantially. Yet results worsened at first. Many experienced teachers took retrenchment packages in 1996, and the school-leaving pass rate fell from **58 per cent in 1994 to 49 per cent in 1998**. A UNESCO study in 2000 found that South African children aged eight and nine had among the worst literacy and numeracy in Africa, which Thompson called a serious omen.

In **health**, the focus shifted from costly city hospitals to clinics and primary health care in deprived areas, reaching thousands who had never had care before. But public hospital standards declined, and those who could afford it moved to private care. The gravest failure was **AIDS**. Neither the apartheid government nor the Government of National Unity took appropriate steps to control the spread of HIV, and Thabo Mbeki, deputy president and then president, questioned the effectiveness of antiretroviral drugs. The historian John Iliffe suggests the rise in HIV could not have been prevented, but experts agree that Mbeki's stance made its impact worse.

This mattered because social policy extended services to millions for the first time, which meant that the quality of those services, rather than access to them, became the main problem.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Millions still lacked water and electricity.
Thousands of new schools were built.

useItInAnEssay.prove: Thousands of new schools were built and primary schooling made compulsory, yet the school-leaving pass rate fell from 58 per cent in 1994 to 49 per cent in 1998.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that more children attended school but learned less, so the skills shortage Thompson warned about persisted.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the problem partly reflected apartheid's legacy of fifteen education departments and under-resourced black schools.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Social policy was therefore a success in access and a failure in quality by 1999.

chunks.title: Two nations? Inequality, land, affirmative action and women
chunks.body:
On 29 May 1998 the deputy president, **Thabo Mbeki**, told parliament that South Africa was "a country of two nations": one white and relatively prosperous, the other black and poor. Reconciliation, he warned, was not being realised. The evidence supported him. About 57 per cent of the population lived below the poverty line in both 1996 and 2001, and the Gini index of inequality rose from 0.69 to 0.77. Meredith (2005) estimates that perhaps 5 per cent of the black community reached middle-class status, while the majority remained poor.

**Land** showed the limits of reform. Nearly four million people had been forcibly removed under apartheid, and in 1994 black farmers controlled only about 16 per cent of arable land. The government aimed to transfer 30 per cent of farmland within five years and set up a Land Claims Commission and a Land Claims Court. But the constitution protected property rights, so owners could not be forced to sell, and less than 2 per cent of land was reallocated in five years.

**Affirmative action** changed the state faster. The government advertised 11,000 affirmative action posts and granted nearly 57,000 early retirement packages by the end of 1998; between 1994 and 1999 the share of civil service posts held by whites fell from 44 to 18 per cent. Black Economic Empowerment aimed to increase black ownership of companies. Historians disagree about the principle: Giliomee and Mbenga argue that affirmative action compromised the constitution's commitment to equality, while Christopher Saunders points out that the constitution itself allowed race-based measures to remedy past injustice.

**Women** gained legal rights. A Commission on Gender Equality was set up, laws covered domestic violence and the right to terminate a pregnancy, and a 1998 law recognising customary marriages ended rural women's status as legal minors, though not their unequal rights to inherit or own communal land. By 2000 women held 30 per cent of the seats in parliament.

This mattered because political equality had been won but economic inequality persisted, which meant that by 2000 democracy had changed who governed South Africa more than how most people lived.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Land reform fell far short of its target.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Urban land claims were largely settled.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Affirmative action transformed the civil service.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Giliomee and Mbenga argue it compromised equality.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that most black South Africans remained poor, so, as Meredith estimates, only perhaps 5 per cent reached the middle class.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, affirmative action cut the white share of civil service posts from 44 to 18 per cent, and welfare reached millions.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Policy therefore reduced inequality in the state, but not in society as a whole.

arguments.claim: Against: refusals and anger from all sides.

modelPlan.counter: Mbeki himself said in 1998 that national reconciliation was not being realised.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did it achieve reconciliation? Truth, yes; reconciliation only in part.

segments.text: The TRC achieved truth more fully than reconciliation.
Between 1996 and 1998 more than 22,000 victims told their stories in hearings broadcast live, and only 1,167 of 7,116 amnesty applications were granted.
This meant that apartheid's crimes could no longer be denied, so Goldstone called it 'a bridge from the old to the new'.
However, Botha refused to appear, the ANC tried to block the report, and many victims felt justice had not been done.
The claim is therefore only partly valid: the TRC made reconciliation possible but did not achieve it.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the success of the social policies of the ANC government between 1994 and 1999.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge

modelPlan.thesis: Social policy succeeded in widening access to welfare, schooling and primary health care, but failed to improve quality, and its response to AIDS was a serious failure.
modelPlan.counter: The legacy of apartheid's fifteen education departments limited what could be achieved in five years.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judged by access, a success; judged by quality, a failure.

segments.text: The ANC government's social policies succeeded in access but failed in quality.
Thousands of new schools were built and primary schooling made compulsory, yet the pass rate fell from 58 per cent in 1994 to 49 per cent in 1998.
This meant that more children attended school without learning more, so the skills shortage persisted.
However, welfare grants and primary health care reached millions who had never had them, though the response to AIDS was a serious failure.
Social policy was therefore a partial success, measured more by who was reached than by what they received.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons for, and the results of, the government's change of economic policy between 1996 and 2000.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.scope: The change from the RDP to GEAR
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which result was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The government replaced the RDP with GEAR because the RDP was unaffordable and it hoped free-market policies would attract investment; the results were stability and growth but continued high unemployment.
modelPlan.counter: COSATU and the SACP opposed the change, which shows it divided the ANC's alliance.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result mattered most? Continued unemployment, which limited the reduction of inequality.

segments.text: The government changed economic policy because the RDP could not be paid for.
In 1996 the RDP office was closed and Trevor Manuel announced GEAR, which included privatisation and aimed to attract overseas investment.
This meant that redistribution gave way to growth, which averaged 3.2 per cent a year with inflation falling to around 6 per cent.
However, COSATU claimed half a million jobs had been lost by 2000, and unemployment remained very high.
The most significant result was therefore a stable economy that still failed to create jobs.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the impact of affirmative action on South African society between 1994 and 1999.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which impact mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Affirmative action rapidly transformed the civil service and helped create a black middle class, but it benefited a small elite and raised disputes about constitutional equality.
modelPlan.counter: Giliomee and Mbenga argue that affirmative action compromised constitutional equality.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which impact mattered most? The transformation of the state, which changed who governed.

segments.text: Affirmative action transformed the state more than society as a whole.

The government advertised 11,000 affirmative action posts and granted nearly 57,000 early retirement packages, and the white share of civil service posts fell from 44 to 18 per cent between 1994 and 1999.
This meant that the civil service began to reflect the population, while Meredith estimates that only perhaps 5 per cent of black South Africans reached the middle class.
However, Giliomee and Mbenga argue it compromised equality, while Saunders notes the constitution allowed such measures.
Affirmative action's main impact was therefore on the state and a new elite, not on the poor majority.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent did the position of women in South Africa improve between 1994 and 2000?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: Law changed faster than custom and the economy

modelPlan.thesis: Women's legal and political position improved substantially, with a gender commission, new laws and 30 per cent of parliamentary seats by 2000, but customary law and economic inequality limited the change for rural women.

arguments.claim: The Commission on Gender Equality and new laws.
Customary marriages law and its limits.

modelPlan.counter: The 1998 law did nothing about women's right to inherit or own communal land.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How far? Far in law and politics; less far for rural women under customary law.

segments.text: The position of women improved substantially in law and politics.
A Commission on Gender Equality was set up, new laws covered domestic violence and the right to terminate pregnancies, and by 2000 women held 30 per cent of seats in parliament.
This meant that women's equality was protected by the state, so their voice in government grew quickly.
However, the 1998 customary marriages law did not give rural women equal rights to inherit or own communal land.
Women's position therefore improved greatly in law, but less for the rural women who were most disadvantaged.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the economic policies of the democratic governments of South Africa and Argentina between 1994 and 1999.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout
decodeKey.judgement: Which succeeded more, and for whom?

modelPlan.thesis: Both governments turned to free-market policies that brought stability but not jobs: South Africa's GEAR and Argentina's Convertibility and privatisation; but South Africa kept strong labour protections, whereas Argentine unions could not resist, and only in Argentina did unemployment help defeat the governing party in 1999.

arguments.claim: Similarity: a turn to free-market policies by parties with other traditions.
Difference: labour protection and political consequences.

modelPlan.counter: Both governments inherited economic crises: South Africa a bankrupt economy in 1994, and Argentina the hyperinflation that Menem's policies eliminated.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which policy succeeded more? Both stabilised the economy; neither created enough jobs.

segments.text: South Africa and Argentina both turned to free-market policies in the 1990s, with similar successes and failures.
South Africa replaced the RDP with GEAR in 1996, including privatisation, whereas Menem privatized most state enterprises and pegged the peso to the dollar in 1991.
This meant that both economies stabilised, with South African inflation falling to around 6 per cent and Argentine hyperinflation eliminated, but unemployment rose in both.
However, South Africa's new labour laws gave unions unusual power, as Thompson notes, whereas Argentine unions were unable to resist, and high unemployment helped defeat the Peronists in 1999.
The policies were therefore similar in their economic results but different in their treatment of organised labour.
